passages.original: 19. Barthius, loc. cit., legendum censet Post praecepta Dei : hoc est. post evocationem, seu, ut Hieronymus loqui amat, dormitionem. Sic frequen- ter in formulis Christianorum testamentorum legi- mus : Cum Dominus de me praeceperit. Quod et ipsum ex stylo sanctorum Patrum traductum. Adde versum 14 hujus carminis : Sed prior uxorem decreti pagina Legit.
passages.english: 19. Barth, in the place cited, thinks we should read "After the commands of God": that is, after [one's] calling away, or, as Jerome likes to put it, [one's] falling asleep. Thus we frequently read in the formulas of Christian wills: "When the Lord shall have given command concerning me." This too was itself taken over from the style of the holy Fathers. Add line 14 of this poem: "But the earlier page of the decree chose a wife."
passages.notes: These are editorial commentary notes on the poem; the numbers refer to its lines. "Barthius" is the scholar Caspar von Barth. "Legit" in the quoted line 14 may mean "chose" or "reads"; the sense is uncertain without the poem.

passages.original: 97. Barthius, libr. xxv, c. 7, affirmat, tueor pas- sive usurpari a Boethio, et ab auctore hujus carmi- nis : quamquam dc hoc certus non erat, cum liber illi ad manum non esset. Si hunc locum innuit, tueri hic accipitur pro intueri active. Sensus enim est : ut nostra ora paterentur te tueri, Genitor te in- duit, etc.
passages.english: 97. Barth, book 25, chapter 7, asserts that *tueor* is used in a passive sense by Boethius and by the author of this poem, although he was not certain about this, since the book was not at hand for him. If he is hinting at this passage, *tueri* is taken here for *intueri* [to look upon] in an active sense. For the meaning is: "so that our faces might bear to look upon you, the Father clothed you," etc.
passages.notes: "dc" is read as "de" (scanning error). The line number 97 refers to the poem being commented on.
